title: How to Prepare for English Literature
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Answering a parent whose daughter is drowning in GCSE revision, Salles argues that English literature teaching creates overload by default and that the fix is ruthless reduction plus deliberate spacing. His diagnosis is that teachers model quote analysis so heavily that students accumulate fifty to a hundred quotations per text, and that fear of being blamed for a wrong prediction stops departments from telling students what actually matters. Against this he proposes starting from the author's purpose, cutting to a set of fifteen to twenty five quotations per text, and rehearsing essay plans rather than full essays. The centerpiece is a lay account of the forgetting curve: memory strengthens only when retrieval happens after a gap, so the gaps should double, running from mid September through to April. He then does the arithmetic to show the whole year's revision costs roughly fifteen hours. The piece closes with concrete per text selections for Romeo and Juliet, Jekyll and Hyde and Lord of the Flies, and a claim that endings and openings repay attention most.
points: Salles blames overload on a teaching habit rather than on student laziness, noting that heavy modelling of quote analysis leaves students with far more material than anyone could memorise.
He reframes revision as building a small transferable core, arguing that three character centered essays per text will cover virtually every question a paper can ask.
The spacing argument is the engine of the piece: retrieval only strengthens memory when a gap has been left, so the intervals should keep doubling across year 11.
He puts numbers on the claim, estimating forty five minutes per essay across the year and about fifteen hours total for twenty essay plans.
He identifies institutional fear of blame as the reason departments refuse to name high value questions, even though only one of seven possible questions will appear.
quotes: It is not unusual to have 50-100 quotes analysed for every text. There are 15 poems in the anthology, and they will have at least 10 quotes analysed each.
But, if you asked that same teacher: how are your students going to learn all these quotes? they'll confess it is too much.

Brains are designed to forget. We would be paralysed with too much information if we remembered everything - it would be impossible to function, like walking through a house in which we had never thrown anything away.

So evolution has created a perfect system. We forget everything, unless our environment asks us to recall it and use it again. When our environment forces us to do this, the brain builds stronger memory.
But, if you leave a gap and then have to remember again, the brain builds a stronger memory. The neural connection carves out a wider path, so it is more easy to find next time you need it.

If there are 7 possible questions that can come up on a text, only one of them will. So, at best we can say that only 15% of what you revise will come up in the exam. 85% of what we tell students to revise won't come up.
Remember, although you are revising only 3 essays per text, you are still revising the top 15, 20 or 25 quotes and analysis - they will cover all characters and themes.
The richest part of every text you ever study for GCSE, A level and university is always the ending. This is where the author ties together all the ideas and themes of the text.
